lesson.title: Introducing yourself
lesson.description: Give a concise, honest introduction suited to the conversation.
learning_objectives: Give a concise, honest introduction suited to the conversation.

sections.title: Goal and intuition
sections.learning_objective: Give a concise, honest introduction suited to the conversation.
sections.markdown: An introduction helps another person understand what you are doing now and why this conversation is relevant. It is not a competition to invent the strongest biography. Choose a small set of true details: current study or role, one concrete piece of work, what you did, and what you want to learn or contribute. Adapt length to the question and allow the other person to ask more.
key_points: Invented experience creates claims you cannot support in follow-up questions.
sections.checkpoint: Can you explain why each step follows from the stated assumptions?

sections.title: A worked example and why it works
sections.learning_objective: Give a concise, honest introduction suited to the conversation.
sections.markdown: Illustrative rehearsal, not a statement about the learner: 'I am studying computer science. In a small notes project I implemented search and wrote tests for empty results. That taught me to check edge cases. I am interested in an entry-level role where I can strengthen my Python and testing skills.' This gives a current context, a checkable action and a learning direction. It does not claim commercial customers or team leadership. A project description should distinguish your own contribution from the group's work.

sections.title: Guided practice, independent practice and revision
sections.learning_objective: Give a concise, honest introduction suited to the conversation.
sections.markdown:
Guided: replace each detail in the example with a true detail of your own; remove any sentence you cannot explain with evidence. Independent: write a short introduction for a placement conversation, then a shorter version for a project discussion.

<details><summary>Self-review questions</summary>Can a listener identify your current context? Is there a specific action you personally took? Have you separated fact from aspiration? Could you explain the project if asked? Is there room for a follow-up? Several clear answers can be equally valid.</details>

Revision: be honest, use concrete actions, avoid unsupported labels, respect the requested length, and ask for clarification when needed. Forge stores this as reflection and supplies a rubric, not an automatic communication score or a prediction of hiring success.
